name: Mughal Empire
tierReason: Rich lands and brilliant early emperors. Rule wisely and tolerantly, and you'll thrive.
summary: Found an empire with gunpowder, unite Hindus and Muslims, and build the Taj Mahal.
intro: You begin as Babur in 1526, a prince from Central Asia invading northern India with cannons and guns, and continue through his descendants Akbar, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb. Your strengths: some of the richest farmland and trade on Earth. Your challenge: a Muslim dynasty ruling over a mostly Hindu population.

collapse.text: Rebellious nobles, angry subjects, and an empty treasury tore your empire apart. Rival kingdoms divided northern India.

survive.text: Your Mughal Empire endures, rich and powerful, into the 1700s.

glossary.def: the dynasty founded by Babur; the name comes from the Persian word for Mongol

Hindu warrior clans who ruled kingdoms in northwestern India

a small spiritual circle of nobles devoted to Akbar as their guide

Hindu warrior people of western India who built their own kingdom

timeline.text: Babur defeats the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat with cannons and matchlock guns, founding the Mughal Empire.
Humayun is driven out of India by Sher Shah Suri, then returns with Persian help.
Akbar allies with the Rajputs, abolishes the jizya (1564), builds the mansabdar system, and promotes "peace with all."
Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal, a symbol of Mughal wealth and power.
Aurangzeb expands the empire to its largest size, but brings back the jizya (1679) and fights endless wars in the Deccan.
Nader Shah of Persia sacks Delhi and carries off the Peacock Throne, speeding the empire's breakup. The British East India Company soon rises in its place.

panipat.title: The Battle of Panipat
panipat.text: You are Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan. You've lost your homeland, but from your base in Kabul you've set your sights on the rich plains of northern India. At Panipat, Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, faces you with a much larger army that includes hundreds of war elephants. Your army is small but battle-tested, and it has something the Sultan's army lacks: field cannons and matchlock guns.

options.text: Tie your carts into a wall, put cannons and matchlock gunners in the gaps, and send cavalry around the sides.
options.explanation: A brilliant victory, and Babur's real plan. His guns terrified the elephants, his cavalry swept around the sides, and Ibrahim Lodi died in battle in 1526. The win founded the Mughal Empire, one of the great gunpowder empires.

options.text: Charge the Sultan's army head-on with your cavalry before it can attack.
options.explanation: Bold, but a head-on charge into a much bigger army with war elephants was a huge gamble. Babur won in 1526 by defending a fortified line with guns and striking from the sides.

options.text: Retreat to Kabul for now. The Sultan's army is far bigger than yours, and one lost battle here could destroy your army and your dream of India. Raid again later, when the odds are better.
options.explanation: Too cautious. Babur had already raided India several times, and this was his moment. His victory at Panipat in 1526 made him ruler of Delhi and Agra.

stay.title: Stay or Go Home?
stay.text: You now hold Delhi, Agra, and the treasure of the Delhi sultans. But your soldiers hate India's heat and want to take their loot home to Kabul. Meanwhile, Rana Sanga, the Rajput king of Mewar, is gathering a huge alliance of Rajputs and Afghans to drive you out.

options.text: Rally your men with a speech and rewards, then stay and beat the Rajputs with your guns.
options.explanation: That's what Babur did. He persuaded his men to stay and beat Rana Sanga's army at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527 using guns behind carts. Babur died in 1530; his son Humayun lost the empire in 1540 but regained it in 1555, and the dynasty lasted until 1857.

options.text: Take the treasure and go home to Kabul. Your soldiers are homesick and miserable in the heat, and a rich army at home beats a shaky throne in India.
options.explanation: You'd win a fortune but lose an empire. Babur chose to stay, and India's wealth made the Mughals one of the richest dynasties in the world.

options.text: Stay in India, but avoid a risky battle with Rana Sanga. Send gold and gifts to the Rajput kings to break up their alliance and buy peace, and save your soldiers for later wars.
options.explanation: Friendship with the Rajputs would matter a lot later, but in 1527 Rana Sanga wanted to drive Babur out entirely. Babur defeated him at the Battle of Khanwa that year.

khanwa.title: The Rajput Challenge
khanwa.text: Your hold on northern India is shaky. Rana Sanga, the Rajput king of Mewar, has gathered a huge alliance of Rajputs and Afghans to drive you out. Your soldiers are frightened; they have heard that Rajput warriors never retreat.

context.text: Your reckless charge at Panipat won the day, but it cost you many of your best soldiers.
After retreating, you came back a year later and finally took Delhi, but you lost precious time.

options.text: Build a fortified line of carts, cannons, and matchlock gunners, and let the Rajputs charge into your guns.
options.explanation: Exactly Babur's tactic. At the Battle of Khanwa in 1527, his guns and flanking cavalry broke Rana Sanga's army. This victory made Babur the strongest ruler in northern India, though his son Humayun lost it in 1540 and only won it back in 1555.

options.text: Make a deal: give the Rajputs half your new lands if they leave you alone. Your frightened soldiers may not stand against warriors who never retreat, and half an empire is better than none.
options.explanation: Giving away half your conquest so early would signal weakness and invite more attacks. Babur instead fought and won at Khanwa in 1527.

options.text: Pull back to Delhi and let the Rajputs wear themselves out.
options.explanation: Waiting lets your enemies grow stronger. Babur faced the Rajputs head-on at Khanwa in 1527 and won with his guns.

humayun.title: Driven Out!
humayun.text: Your weak start has caught up with your family. Babur's son Humayun is now emperor, and in 1540 an Afghan leader named Sher Shah Suri defeats him and seizes northern India. Humayun flees west with only a few followers. The Mughal Empire is close to disappearing.

options.text: Take refuge with the Shah of Persia, borrow Persian troops, and return to win back the empire.
options.explanation: This is what really happened (even though Babur had won his battles). Humayun lived in exile with the Safavid Shah Tahmasp, returned with Persian troops to take Kabul in 1545, and finally retook Delhi in 1555, shortly before he died. Persian artists and officials who joined him shaped Mughal culture for centuries.

options.text: Give up and retire to Kabul as a minor prince.
options.explanation: That would end the Mughal story. Humayun refused to quit: he went into exile in Persia, came back with Persian troops, and recaptured Delhi in 1555.

options.text: Hide in the deserts of Sindh with your loyal followers and raid Sher Shah's lands. Quick raids keep your name alive and wear him down until people are ready to welcome you back.
options.explanation: Raiding could keep your name alive, but not win back an empire. Humayun eventually got real help from Persia's Shah Tahmasp and retook Delhi in 1555.

akbar.title: Akbar and the Rajputs
akbar.text: You are Akbar, Babur's grandson, who became emperor at just 13 years old in 1556. You are a Muslim ruler, but most of your subjects are Hindus, and the proud Rajput kings control key forts and the roads to the sea. Your Muslim nobles expect you to keep collecting the jizya from Hindus. How will you win over, or win against, the people you rule?

context.text: Because Babur went home to Kabul, your family had to fight its way back into India, and many Indians still see you as foreign invaders.

options.text: Most of your subjects are Hindus, so make the Rajput kings your partners: marry into their families, give them high ranks as generals and governors, and abolish the jizya.
options.explanation: Brilliant, and Akbar's real policy. He married a Rajput princess in 1562, made Rajput kings top generals and governors, and abolished the jizya in 1564. Many Rajputs became the empire's most loyal defenders.

options.text: Conquer the Rajputs by force and keep collecting the jizya, as your Muslim nobles expect. Proud kings must learn to obey.
options.explanation: Force alone was costly. Akbar did besiege Rajput forts that refused his alliances, but his main strategy was partnership, including abolishing the jizya in 1564. That turned rivals into loyal commanders.

options.text: Require all of your subjects to convert to Islam.
options.explanation: That would have turned millions of Hindus against you. Akbar did the opposite, abolishing the jizya in 1564 and welcoming Hindus into high government posts.

ibadat.title: The House of Worship
ibadat.text: Your new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, is a showcase of red sandstone palaces. You are curious about every religion in your empire, so you build a hall called the House of Worship. At first only Muslim scholars debate there, but soon you invite Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, and even Jesuit priests from Portuguese Goa.

options.text: Open the debates to all faiths and promote 'peace with all' (sulh-i kul).
options.explanation: Exactly Akbar's approach. His debates and his policy of sulh-i kul helped hold a very diverse empire together. He also created a small spiritual circle called Din-i Ilahi for a few nobles, but he never forced it on anyone.

options.text: Blend the best ideas of every faith into one new religion, make yourself its guide, and order all your subjects to join it so the whole empire shares one belief.
options.explanation: Too far. Akbar's small spiritual circle, Din-i Ilahi, was only for a few loyal nobles and faded after he died. Forcing everyone to join would have angered Muslims and Hindus alike.

options.text: Close the hall. The debates are stirring up controversy, and only Sunni scholars should advise the emperor on matters of faith.
options.explanation: That would please some strict scholars but alienate the Hindu and Shia nobles your empire depended on. Akbar instead opened the debates to every faith and promoted "peace with all."

chittor.title: The Siege of Chittor
chittor.text: Many Rajput kings refuse to bow to you. The great fortress of Chittor, home of the Rajput kingdom of Mewar, has closed its gates. Your army has cannons and skilled siege engineers, but every month of siege costs money, and the Rajputs are famous for fighting to the last.

options.text: Take the fort, then offer every other Rajput king a generous alliance: high rank in your army, marriage ties to your family, and an end to the jizya.
options.explanation: Smart: tough when needed, generous when possible. Akbar did capture Chittor in 1568 after a brutal siege, but his real success came from alliances with Rajput kings and from abolishing the jizya in 1564.

options.text: Take the fort, then destroy every Rajput kingdom one by one.
options.explanation: Endless war against proud warriors would drain your treasury. Even after Chittor fell in 1568, Mewar kept resisting for decades, so Akbar relied on alliances with other Rajput kings.

options.text: Give up the siege and leave the Rajputs alone. They are famous for fighting to the last, and every month here drains men and money.
options.explanation: Leaving powerful enemies untouched near your capital is dangerous. Akbar took Chittor in 1568 and then won over most Rajput kings through alliances.

mansabdar.title: Running a Giant Empire
mansabdar.text: Your empire now stretches across northern India and is home to many millions of people. You need officers, soldiers, and a way to collect taxes from millions of farmers without letting nobles grow too powerful. Your finance minister, Raja Todar Mal, a Hindu, has an idea: measure the land and set taxes based on average harvests.

context.text: Your Rajput allies now lead some of your best armies.

options.text: Give Muslim and Hindu nobles ranks called mansabs, pay them with land-tax rights that move every few years, and set fair taxes with Todar Mal's survey.
options.explanation: This is Akbar's real system. Mansabdars supplied soldiers and were paid from land taxes they could not keep forever, so no noble could build a private kingdom. Local landholders called zamindars collected the taxes, based on Todar Mal's careful surveys.

options.text: Give each noble a permanent family estate to rule as he sees fit.
options.explanation: Permanent estates would let nobles build private power bases and someday challenge you. Akbar made sure mansabdars were moved around and could not pass their land rights to their sons.

options.text: Set one high tax on every farm, whether the harvest is good or bad. A single fixed rate is simple to collect, hard to cheat, and gives the treasury the same income every year.
options.explanation: Flat high taxes would ruin farmers in bad years and spark revolts. Todar Mal's system based taxes on surveys of land and average crop yields, which made collection fairer and more reliable.

taj.title: A Monument for the Ages
taj.text: You are Shah Jahan, Akbar's grandson. Your empire is one of the richest on Earth, and its cotton cloth is sold from Southeast Asia to Europe. In 1631 your beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died. You want to honor her and show the world your dynasty's glory. Your treasury is full, but some advisers want the money spent on conquering your ancestors' homeland in Central Asia.

options.text: Build the Taj Mahal and a new capital at Delhi, and keep your finances in order.
options.explanation: Monuments like these showed the power and legitimacy of Mughal rule. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal (about 1632–1653), which blends Persian, Islamic, and Indian styles, plus a new capital at Delhi with the Red Fort and the jeweled Peacock Throne.

options.text: Skip the buildings and spend the money conquering Central Asia, your ancestors' homeland. Winning it would bring more glory than any tomb.
options.explanation: Shah Jahan did try this in 1646–1647: his armies took the city of Balkh in 1646 but had to withdraw in 1647 after huge expenses. The Taj Mahal, which he also built, proved a far better investment in Mughal prestige.

options.text: Save all the money. Grand buildings cost a fortune, and even with a full treasury, a wise ruler keeps reserves for wars, famines, and hard times ahead.
options.explanation: Saving is sensible, but monuments helped legitimize rule by showing power, faith, and wealth. Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal (about 1632–1653) still symbolizes the Mughal golden age.

aurangzeb.title: Aurangzeb's Choice
aurangzeb.text: You are Aurangzeb, Shah Jahan's son. You seized the throne in 1658 after a bloody war against your brothers and imprisoned your father. You are a devout Sunni Muslim who wants your empire to follow strict Islamic law, and religious advisers urge you to bring back the jizya on Hindus. Meanwhile, the Hindu Marathas are rising in the south, and the Sikhs are growing stronger in the Punjab.

context.text: For over a century, Akbar's alliances with the Rajputs have kept the peace and filled your armies with loyal Hindu commanders.
The Rajput kings have never fully trusted your dynasty.
Akbar's policy of 'peace with all' is still remembered fondly by Hindus, Sikhs, and Shia Muslims.

options.text: Keep Akbar's tolerant policies: no jizya, no temple destruction, and respect for all faiths. With the Marathas and Sikhs on the rise, you need your Hindu allies loyal.
options.explanation: This would have kept your Hindu allies loyal. Instead, Aurangzeb brought back the jizya in 1679 and destroyed some Hindu temples, which angered Rajputs, Marathas, and Sikhs and fueled revolts that weakened the empire.

options.text: Bring back the jizya and enforce strict Islamic law across the empire. You are a devout ruler, and your religious advisers say it is your duty.
options.explanation: This is what Aurangzeb really did in 1679. He also executed the Sikh leader Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675) and destroyed some Hindu temples. These policies turned many former allies into enemies.

options.text: Live by strict Islamic rules at court, but don't tax or punish non-Muslims for their faith.
options.explanation: A workable middle path: a ruler could be personally devout without alienating his subjects. Aurangzeb instead brought back the jizya in 1679, and resentment helped fuel the revolts that weakened Mughal rule.

deccan.title: War in the Deccan
deccan.text: Your empire has reached its largest size ever, covering almost all of India. But in the Deccan, the Maratha kingdom founded by the warrior-king Shivaji keeps fighting. The Marathas avoid big battles; they raid supply lines and slip away into the hills. Your generals say victory needs just a few more years.

options.text: Make peace: let Maratha leaders rule their lands as your allies, paying tribute and sending you soldiers. Chasing raiders through the hills has cost enough.
options.explanation: A realistic choice that would have saved men and money. Instead, Aurangzeb spent his last 26 years fighting in the Deccan; the endless war emptied the treasury, and after his death in 1707 the empire began to break apart.

options.text: Keep fighting until every Maratha fort is taken, however long it takes.
options.explanation: This is what Aurangzeb did, staying in the Deccan from 1681 until his death in 1707. The war drained the treasury while the Marathas grew stronger, and after 1707 Mughal power declined quickly.

options.text: Pull your armies back and defend only the north. The Deccan war is swallowing men and money, and the rich northern heartland matters most.
options.explanation: Safer than endless war, but giving up the south without a deal could encourage other rebels. Aurangzeb chose to fight on until his death in 1707, a costly decision that weakened the empire.

revolts.title: Revolts Everywhere
revolts.text: Your strict policies have stirred up resistance across the empire. The Marathas raid in the south, Rajput kings have rebelled, Sikhs are arming themselves in the Punjab, and Jat farmers have revolted near Agra. Your treasury shrinks as the wars spread.

options.text: Cancel the jizya, stop destroying temples, and negotiate with the rebels.
options.explanation: Returning to Akbar's approach would have calmed many rebels. Aurangzeb never changed course, and after his death in 1707 the empire weakened quickly; in 1739 the Persian ruler Nader Shah sacked Delhi.

options.text: Crush every rebellion with force, no matter the cost: march against the Marathas, the Rajputs, the Sikhs, and the Jat farmers, one after another.
options.explanation: Close to what Aurangzeb tried. Fighting rebels on every side drained the treasury, and after his death in 1707 Mughal power broke up into rival kingdoms.

options.text: Hand large regions over to governors and let them deal with the rebels, so your own armies can focus on the biggest threats.
options.explanation: This might keep some peace, but it lets governors become nearly independent rulers. That is exactly what happened after 1707, when provinces like Bengal and Hyderabad broke away.
